title: My family
seoTitle: Turkish possessive suffixes and how to say have
intro: This unit gives Turkish nouns their owners. A suffix says whose something is: *ev* (house) → *evim* (my house), *evin* (your house). With *var* and *yok*, the same suffixes are how Turkish says **have**: *Arabam var* (I have a car). You'll also meet two sound changes these suffixes bring out: vowel loss (*ağız* → *ağzım*) and softening (*kitap* → *kitabım*).

blocks.text: Turkish has no separate words for **my**, **your** or **his**. A possessive suffix (*iyelik eki*) on the noun does the job, one for each person, in four-way harmony. After a consonant the suffix starts with a vowel: *evim*. After a vowel that vowel drops, *arabam*, and in the third person a buffer *s* appears instead: *arabası*.
The I follows four-way harmony with the last vowel of the noun, as with **to be** in [unit 3](gp-harmony-4way):

**Their.** `-lArI` means **their**: *evleri* (their house). The same form also means **his houses** and **their houses**: Turkish doesn't add a second plural, so context decides. A plural owned noun takes the plural first: *evlerim* (my houses), *kitapların* (your books).

**With case endings.** A case ending comes after the possessive: *evimde* (in my house), *evime* (to my house), *evimden* (from my house), *arabanı* (your car, as an object). After **his** or **her**, an extra n slips in before the case (*evinde*, in his house); [unit 10](gp-pronominal-n) explains it.

items.en: Are you coming to our house?

blocks.text: English and French put the owner in front, **my** or mon, ma, mes; Turkish puts it at the end. For emphasis you can add a pronoun in front, *benim evim* (**my** house), as in *Benim adım…* from unit 1. These pronouns, *benim, senin, onun*, come in [unit 10](gp-genitive).

*Evi* can be **his house** or **the house** as an object (the accusative of [unit 8](gp-accusative)): *Evi büyük* (His house is big), *Evi seviyorum* (I love the house). After a vowel the two look different: *arabası* (his car), *arabayı* (the car).

sections.title: Arabam var: how to say have

blocks.text: Turkish has no verb for **have**. It says that the owned thing exists: *Arabam var*, literally **my car exists**, means **I have a car**. *Yok* says that it doesn't: *Arabam yok* (I don't have a car).

Questions take `mI` as in [unit 5](gp-var-yok): *Kardeşin var mı?* (Do you have brothers or sisters?) *Evet, var.* (Yes, I do.) *Hayır, yok.* (No, I don't.) Note that the short answers need no ending: *var* and *yok* are enough.

items.en: I have two brothers and sisters.

blocks.text: *Bir* in front of the owned thing is usual when you introduce it: *Bir sorum var*, *Bir kedim var*. With things people usually have just one of, or that aren't counted, leave it out: *Arabam var*, *Zamanım yok*, *Param yok*.
For **he** or **she** the third-person suffix is enough: *Arabası var* (She has a car). To name the owner, *Ayşe'nin arabası var*, you need the genitive of [unit 10](gp-genitive-possessive).

Don't look for a verb: *Ben bir araba var* is wrong. The owner goes into the suffix: *Bir arabam var*. And possession takes *yok*, not *değil*: *Arabam yok* (I don't have a car), but *Arabam değil* (It isn't my car).

A small group of two-syllable words, many of them parts of the body or loanwords from Arabic, drop the vowel of their last syllable when a suffix that starts with a vowel follows. This is vowel loss (*ünlü düşmesi*): *ağız* (mouth) → *ağzım* (my mouth).

It happens before every suffix that starts with a vowel, not only the possessive: *şehre* (to the city), *resmi* (the picture, as an object). Before a suffix that starts with a consonant the word stays whole: *şehirde*, *şehirler*, *resimden*.

**Doubled consonants.** A few Arabic loanwords double their last consonant before a vowel instead: *hak* (right) → *hakkım* (my right), *his* (feeling) → *hissim*, *sır* (secret) → *sırrı*. The adjective *haklı* (right, in the right) from [unit 4](a1-u04) has a consonant suffix, so it keeps one k.

Most words don't lose a vowel: *kalem* → *kalemim*, *okul* → *okulum*, *defter* → *defterim*. Vowel loss belongs to particular words, and dictionaries mark it: *ağız, -ğzı*. Learn the common ones as you meet them.
*Vakit* and *zaman* both mean **time**, and both are everyday words: *Vaktin var mı?* and *Zamanın var mı?* ask the same thing.

After a consonant, the possessive suffixes start with a vowel, so they bring out the softening of [unit 8](gp-consonant-softening): p → b, ç → c, t → d, k → ğ. The same words keep their consonant as before: most one-syllable words, and names.
Only the forms with a vowel soften. **Their** starts with a consonant, so the stem stays: *kitapları* (their book), *çocukları* (their child).

**Su and ne.** *Su* (water) takes a *y* where you'd expect the buffer s: *suyum* (my water), *suyun*, *suyu*. *Ne* (what) does the same in a useful phrase: *Neyin var?* (What's wrong with you?, literally what do you have?).
*Çocuğunuz var mı?* asks about one child or several: Turkish keeps the noun singular in questions like this, where English says **children**.

summary: Possessive suffixes: `-(I)m, -(I)n, -(s)I, -(I)mIz, -(I)nIz, -lArI`: *evim, evin, evi, evimiz, eviniz, evleri*.
After a vowel, the I drops (*arabam*) and the third person takes a buffer s (*arabası*).
Case endings come after the possessive: *evimde, evime, evimden*.
To have: owned noun + *var* or *yok*: *Arabam var*, *Zamanım yok*, *Kardeşin var mı?*
Some words lose a vowel before a vowel suffix: *ağzım, burnu, oğlum, ismim, şehre*. A few double a consonant: *hakkım*.
Possessives soften p, ç, t, k like other vowel suffixes: *kitabım, çocuğumuz, köpeğin*. *Su* gives *suyum*.
